Think white pepper dusted over lemon zest, with none of the darkness of black pepper or the sweetness of pink pepper. Underneath, a soft citrus-floral sweetness emerges, closer to petitgrain than to bergamot — warmer, less bitter, with a faint woody undertow.

Less green than cardamom, less sweet than fennel, less animalic than cumin. On skin, it settles into a gentle, almost powdery linalool signature — clean linen with a whisper of toasted seed. The dry-down is notably discreet, fading within hours rather than persisting, which is precisely why it functions as a blender rather than a protagonist.

Indicative 2025 wholesale prices.

Coriander seed oil is one of perfumery's most underestimated raw materials. Steam-distilled from the dried fru its of Coriandrum sativum (Apiaceae), it delivers 60–80% (+)-linalool — the same molecule that dominates lavender and rosewood, but here in a drier, more angular presentati on. The enantiomeric ratio runs roughly 87% (+)-linalool to 13% (−)-linalool. Minor components include gamm a-terpinene (2–14%), alph a-pinene (0.3–11%), camph or (up to 5.5%), and geranyl acetate (2–40%, highly variable by orig in), which together build the oil's particular peppery-woody opening and soft, almost candy-like floral heart.

The plant is native to the eastern Mediterranean basin. Major producing regions include Russia, India, Morocco, Egypt, and Moldova. Russian and Eastern European origins tend toward higher linalool content and a cleaner, more transparent profile. Indian coriander reads heavier, with more camphoraceous undertones. Egyptian material, grown in the Nile Delta's alluvial soils, often splits the difference — warm and rounded.

The confusion between coriander seed (dry, spicy-citrus) and coriander leaf or cilantro (green, soapy, aldehydic) deserves clarification. They are the same plant but yield completely different olfactory materials. The leaf's polarising soapy quality comes from unsaturated aldehydes — primarily (E)-2-decenal and (E)-2-dodecenal — that are absent from the seed oil. These are not the same as decanal or dodecanal; the unsaturation at the 2-position is what produces the characteristic soapy-metallic sensation that activates the OR6A2 olfactory receptor in genetically sensitive individuals.

In formulation, coriander seed oil is a top-to-heart blender of notable range. Its high linalool content makes it compatible with almost any material. It smooths transitions between citrus and floral zones, rounds out sharp edges in aromatic compositions, and introduces a quiet, dry spiciness to chypre and fougère structures. The oil's substantivity is moderate — approximately 8 hours on blotter at full concentration — which is why perfumers reach for it as a connector rather than a statement note.

Related: Allspice · Anethole · Anise · Asafoetida · Baking Spices · Bay Leaf · Biryani · Caraway

Extraction method: Steam distillation of the dried, crushed fruits (commonly called seeds) of Coriandrum sativum. Crushing immediately before distillation is critical — pre-crushed material loses monoterpenes rapidly. Oil yield ranges from 0.3% to 1.1% depending on cultivar, maturity, and crushing method. Lighter crushing yields approximately 95% of maximum oil in 22 minutes; heavier crushing requires 35–40 minutes. The oil is a colorless to pale yellow, mobile liquid. A CO₂ extract also exists, offering a fuller, more spice-forward profile with better preservation of heat-sensitive compounds.

↑ See Terroir & Origins for origin-specific methods.

Coriander seed oil functions as a top-to-heart blender — a adaptable bridging materials in a perfumer's palette. Its dominant (+)-linalool content (typically 60–80%) gives it native compatibility with florals: rose, neroli, lily of the valley, lavender. Its peppery terpenic qualities (gamm a-terpinene, alph a-pinene) anch or it to citrus and aromatic-herbal zones. In chypre compositions, coriander eases the bergamot-oakmoss transiti on without adding sweetness. In fougères, it reinforces the aromatic spine alongside lavender and coumar in. In fresh masculine constructions, it introduces dry spice without weight or darkness. The oil is IFRA-compliant at up to 10% in fragrance concentrate, with sensitizati on flagged as the critical effect — primarily due to linalool content and potential peroxide formati on during aging. Storage under nitrogen or with antioxidants is standard industry practice.

category: WOODS AND MOSSES  /  woody · earthy · warm
short_description: Dry, faintly musty, mineral-woody. Cork smells like what it is — compressed bark with a dusty, slightly tannic quality. The smell of a freshly pulled wine cork, before the wine.

technical_card.Appearance: Tincture: pale amber liquid with earthy, woody, slightly musty character

evolution.Immediately: Dry, faintly musty, mineral-bark
evolution.After a few hours: Quieter, warmer, woody-waxy
evolution.After a few days: Barely perceptible dry woody residue

extracted_text_body:
Dry, faintly musty, mineral-woody. Cork smells like what it is — compressed bark with a dusty, slightly tannic quality. The smell of a freshly pulled wine cork, before the wine.

Dry, faintly musty, mineral-woody, with a light tannic quality. Not aromatic in the conventional sense — quiet, muted, bark-like. Like holding a fresh wine cork to your nose before the wine has perfumed it — dry, dusty, faintly woody, with that specific suberin-waxy quality unique to cork bark.

Cork (Quercus suber bark) has a particular, muted aromatic character: dry, faintly musty, mineral, with a light woody-tannic quality. The scent is subtle — cork is more notable for what it absorbs (wine aromas, in particular) than for what it emits.

The volatile compounds in cork include 2,4,6-trichloroanisole (TCA — the infamous 'cork taint' molecule, detectable at 2-5 parts per trillion), guaiacol (smoky), vanillin (sweet), and various sesquiterpenes. TCA, when present, overwhelms all other volatiles — it is the musty, wet-cardboard smell that ruins an estimated 3-5% of wine bottles.

Quercus suber is native to the western Mediterranean — Portugal produces approximately 50% of the world's cork. The bark is harvested every 9-12 years without killing the tree, making cork a sustainable natural materials.

In perfumery, cork provides a dry, mineral, woody-bark note — useful in wine-inspired accords, natural compositions, and Mediterranean terroir notes.

Related: Alder · Alpha Humulene · Amaranth · Amberever · Ambramone · Amburana Bark · Antillone · Apple Tree

Extraction method: No standard commercial cork extraction for perfumery. CO2 extraction of Quercus suber bark could produce an aromatic extract but is not standard practice. Cork tincture (bark macerated in alcohol) is used by some artisan perfumers. The note is typically reconstructed from synthetic materials.

Cork provides a dry, mineral, woody-bark modifier. Functions in wine-inspired accords, natural-terroir compositions, and Mediterranean notes. Reconstructed from dry wood materials, faint musty modifiers, and mineral notes. The suberin (cork's waxy polymer) contributes a specific dry, waxy quality. Not commercially extracted for perfumery — the note is reconstructed.

category: FRUITS, VEGETABLES AND NUTS  /  sweet · green · creamy
short_description: Pale, starchy sweetness — raw corn husk, warm hay, a faint vegetal milkiness. Not the butter-and-salt of cooked corn. This is the raw silk itself: blond, dry, and faintly green, like holding sun-warmed plant fibers to your nose.

technical_card.Producing Countries: United States, China, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico

evolution.Immediately: Faint green-starchy snap, like breaking a fresh corn husk. A brief vegetal sharpness from monoterpenes.
evolution.After a few hours: The green recedes. Dry, hay-like warmth settles — coumarin-adjacent, slightly powdery, with a clean grain sweetness.
evolution.After a few days: Barely perceptible: a soft, warm, starchy trace on fabric. More texture than scent — blond, dry, almost invisible.

extracted_text_body:
Pale, starchy sweetness — raw corn husk, warm hay, a faint vegetal milkiness. Not the butter-and-salt of cooked corn. This is the raw silk itself: blond, dry, and faintly green, like holding sun-warmed plant fibers to your nose.

Pale starchy sweetness with a dry, hay-like warmth. Not buttery, not cooked — this is the raw vegetal fiber, closer to dried grass than to popcorn. A faint milky-green quality sits underneath, softer and less sharp than cis-3-hexenol, warmer and less crystalline than heliotropin alone. The overall impression is blond and textile: sun-dried linen, corn husk, warm straw. Compared to oat or rice notes (which tend toward creamier, more lactonic profiles), corn silk reads drier and slightly more vegetal. No floral character. No fruit.

Corn silk — the stigma and style of Zea mays — is a fantasy note in perfumery. No commercial essential oil or absolute exists. The material is not distilled, extracted, or traded as a fragrance raw material. When a perfumer lists 'corn silk,' they are building an accord from scratch: a reconstruction of what fresh corn silk smells like, assembled from available molecules.

The chemistry of actual corn silk volatiles has been studied. El-Ghorab et al. (Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 2007) identified 36 compounds by GC-MS in Egyptian corn silk, dominated by cis-alpha-terpineol (24.2%), 6,11-oxidoacor-4-ene (18.1%), citronellol (16.2%), trans-pinocamphone (5.9%), and eugenol (4.4%). Earlier, Flath et al. (1978) catalogued corn silk volatiles as attractants for Heliothis zea (corn earworm moth). These studies describe a terpene-rich, faintly rosy-herbaceous profile — quite different from the buttery sweetness most people associate with corn, which comes from dimethyl sulfide formed during cooking.

A perfumer reconstructing a corn silk accord would likely work with materials that suggest starchy sweetness, dry vegetal warmth, and blond-hay tonality: ethyl maltol for grain sweetness, coumarin for the hay quality, a trace of heliotropin for powdery softness, perhaps cis-3-hexenyl acetate for green freshness, and a clean musk base for the silky-textile impression. The result is a quiet, transparent accord — not a statement note but a textural modifier that carries warmth and softness without identifiable florality or fruitiness.

Corn silk also has a long history outside perfumery. Known as stigma maydis in pharmacology, it has been used as a diuretic in Native American, Chinese, and Turkish traditional medicine for centuries. Modern pharmacological research (Hasanudin et al., 2012) confirms its flavonoid and phenolic acid content — compounds with documented antioxidant activity, though irrelevant to its olfactory use.

Related: Acerola · Akebia Fruit · Allyl Amyl Glycolate · Arctic Bramble · Argan · Berries · Black Sapote · Buriti

Extraction method: No commercial extraction exists for perfumery use. Corn silk is a fantasy note — its scent is reconstructed as a synthetic accord. GC-MS analysis of raw corn silk volatiles (El-Ghorab et al., J. Agric. Food Chem., 2007) identified 36 compounds in the dichloromethane extract, dominated by cis-alpha-terpineol (24.2%), citronellol (16.2%), and eugenol (4.4%). However, these analytical data describe the plant tissue's volatile profile, not a commercially available extract. No steam distillation, solvent extraction, or CO2 extraction of corn silk is practiced at industrial scale.

Fantasy note — no natural extract exists. Corn silk functions as a textural modifier in gourmand, grain-inspired, and soft-floral compositions. It provides starchy warmth and a dry, hay-adjacent sweetness without the density of vanilla or the sharpness of green notes. In practice, the accord is built from materials like ethyl maltol (grain sweetness), coumarin (hay, dried grass), heliotropin (powdery softness), and clean musks (textile warmth). The note occupies the heart-to-base register, lending quiet volume and a sense of sun-warmed softness. It works with lactonic peach notes, oat milk accords, linen musks, and tonka bean. No Première Peau fragrance currently features a corn silk accord.

category: FLOWERS  /  floral · aromatic · green
short_description: Dry, honeyed, and subtly herbaceous. A warm, powdery sweetness from dried Centaurea flower heads -- less floral than expected, more like dried hay dusted with pollen.

technical_card.Appearance: Fine to coarse brown-grey seeds; extract is pale yellow to amber liquid

evolution.Immediately: Soft, honeyed, pollen-like. A quiet, dry sweetness with herbal undertones.
evolution.After a few hours: The honey softens. Dry hay and chamomile-like warmth remain.
evolution.After a few days: A faint, warm, herbaceous trace. Subtle and natural.

extracted_text_body:
Dry, honeyed, and subtly herbaceous. A warm, powdery sweetness from dried Centaurea flower heads -- less floral than expected, more like dried hay dusted with pollen.

Dry, honeyed, and pollen-dusted. Not the bright blue freshness you might expect. More like a handful of dried cornflowers crumbled between the palms -- warm, papery, with a sweet, hay-like herbaceousness and a faint bitter edge from the green stems.

Cornflower (Centaurea cyanus), also known as sultan seeds or bachelor's button, is a wildflower native to Europe that has been associated with grain fields for millennia. In perfumery, the dried flower heads (seeds) are occasionally used to produce a rare absolute or tincture, though production is extremely limited.

The aromatic profile of cornflower differs significantly from what the vivid blue petals might suggest. There is no bright floral burst. Instead, the scent is dry, honeyed, and herbaceous -- closer to dried hay, chamomile, or immortelle than to any fresh-cut flower. The pollen-like sweetness is gentle and matte, with a faintly bitter, herbal undertone.

In perfumery, cornflower functions as a quiet heart note, contributing a natural, meadow-like quality to floral, herbaceous, and pastoral compositions. It is not a dramatic ingredient -- its role is atmospheric, evoking open fields and warm summer afternoons.

The note is most commonly recreated synthetically, as genuine cornflower absolute is prohibitively rare and expensive. Perfumers approximate its character using combinations of chamomile, honey accords, and dried-hay materials.

—

Related: Accord Eudora · African Marigold · Alpha Amylcinnamaldehyde · Alyssum · Angels Trumpet · Aquaflora · Ashoka Flower · Aurantiol

Extraction method: Solvent extraction of dried flower heads yields a rare absolute. Production is extremely limited and not commercially standardized. Most perfumers work with synthetic reconstructions.

Heart note in pastoral, meadow-floral, and herbaceous compositions. Functions as an atmospheric ingredient, contributing honeyed-herbal warmth and a dried-flower naturalism. Rarely sourced as genuine absolute; typically reconstructed from chamomile, honey accords, and coumarin-adjacent hay materials. Used in compositions evoking wildflower fields and summer landscapes.

category: POPULAR AND WEIRD  /  floral · fruity · rich
short_description: Rich, warm, powdery macrocyclic musk with a subtle fruity layered. Structurally a ketone like muscone, but creamier and with a faint ambergr is-like sweetness.

technical_card.Appearance: Colorless to pale yellow clear liquid

evolution.Immediately: Rich musky burst with powdery-fruity top
evolution.After a few hours: Warm creamy musk, ambergris-like sweetness
evolution.After a few days: Persistent skin-close musk, extremely long-lasting

extracted_text_body:
Rich, warm, powdery macrocyclic musk with a subtle fruity layered. Structurally a ketone like muscone, but creamier and with a faint ambergr is-like sweetness.

Rich, warm, intensely musky with a creamy powdery body. Warmer than Galaxolide, less clean than Habanolide, more animalic-sweet than either. A faint fruity lift separates it from the purely skin-like quality of muscone.

Cosmone (CAS 10461-98-0) is a macrocyclic musk ketone, specifically (5E)-3-methylcyclotetradec-5-en-1-one. It belongs to the same structural family as muscone and civetone rather than the lactone family of ambrettolide.

The scent is intense and diffusive: a rich, warm musk with powdery qualities and a faint fruity layered. It carries an ambergr is-like sweetness similar to of nitro musks but without their regulatory concerns. Effective at 0.1% concentrati on.

Cosmone functions as a base note and fixative. It provides musky radiance and sillage to virtually any composition.

—

Related: Accord Eudora · African Marigold · Alpha Amylcinnamaldehyde · Alyssum · Angels Trumpet · Aquaflora · Ashoka Flower · Aurantiol

Extraction method: Fully synthetic.

Base note and fixative with powerful diffusion. CAS 10461-98-0. Macrocyclic ketone musk effective at 0.1%. Provides musky radiance across all fragrance families. Comparable to muscone and civetone but with additional creamy-ambergris sweetness.

category: FLOWERS  /  floral · fresh · green
short_description: Light, airy, and faintly chocolatey. Cosmos sulphureus smells of cocoa and vanilla; Cosmos bipinnatus is greener and simpler. A wildflower that whispers where others shout.

technical_card.Appearance: Pink, white, or crimson petals (no commercial extract)

evolution.Immediately: Faint, sweet, chocolatey-vanillic (C. atrosanguineus) or green-honeyed (C. bipinnatus). Barely detectable.
evolution.After a few hours: Nearly imperceptible. A soft, warm, vanillic trace if present at all.
evolution.After a few days: Gone. The note is extremely volatile and light.

extracted_text_body:
Light, airy, and faintly chocolatey. Cosmos sulphureus smells of cocoa and vanilla; Cosmos bipinnatus is greener and simpler. A wildflower that whispers where others shout.

Barely there. A whisper of chocolate-vanillic sweetness (from Cosmos atrosanguineus) or a breath of green-honeyed air (from C. bipinnatus). Like leaning into a meadow of cosmos flowers on a still morning and catching, just for a second, something soft, sweet, and almost imaginary.

Cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus, Cosmos sulphureus) is a wildflower native to Mexico, now naturalized worldwide. The genus belongs to the daisy family (Asteraceae). In perfumery, cosmos is a rare and unusual note because the flower's scent is almost imperceptibly faint -- most people cannot smell it without pressing their nose directly into the bloom.

The chocolate cosmos (Cosmos atrosanguineus) is the most aromatically notable species: its dark burgundy flowers produce a genuine chocolate-vanilla scent, driven by vanillin and related compounds. This species is nearly extinct in the wild (all cultivated specimens derive from a single surviving clone) and is not extracted for perfumery.

The more common Cosmos sulphureus has a faint, sweet, slightly cocoa-like character. Cosmos bipinnatus is even lighter -- greenish, barely perceptible, with a honey-like whisper.

In perfumery, cosmos is a fantasy accord that aims to capture this extreme delicacy: a floral note so light it barely exists. Perfumers build it using trace amounts of chocolate/vanillic elements, transparent florals, and green notes at very low concentrations.

—

Related: Abelia · Almond Blossom · Alpha Terpineol · Alstroemeria · Alumroot · Amarillys · Amazon Moonflower · Amethyst Flower

Extraction method: Not commercially extracted. Cosmos flowers yield no viable essential oil or absolute. The note is a fantasy accord built from vanillic, green, and transparent floral materials.

Heart note in delicate floral, wildflower-meadow, and transparent compositions. Functions as a near-subliminal sweetness -- it adds a barely perceptible cocoa-vanillic or green-honeyed warmth without weight. Built from trace vanillin, transparent musks, light green notes, and honey accords. Used where extreme delicacy is the goal.

category: ANIMALICS  /  woody · earthy · warm
short_description: Wet fur drying in sun. Scalp oil on a warm pillowcase. Costus root smells like the human body before soap existed — mammalian, earthy, hairy — then softens into roasted hazelnuts and dark cocoa.

technical_card.Botanical: Dolomiaea costus (syn. Saussurea costus, Saussurea lappa)
technical_card.Appearance: Pale yellow to brownish amber viscous oil (EO); brownish amber semi-solid (absolute)

evolution.Immediately: Raw animal confrontation. Wet fur, human scalp warmed by sun, damp turned earth. Heavy, greasy, enveloping. The sesquiterpene lactones hit as a sharp, almost metallic edge beneath the warmth.
evolution.After a few hours: The aldehydes dissipate. What remains is creamy, nutty — roasted hazelnuts, cocoa nibs, a powdery orris-like smoothness. The animalic quality becomes intimate rather than aggressive. The waxy aplotaxene undertone anchors everything.
evolution.After a few days: A persistent, smooth, skin-like residue. Warm, slightly sweet, profoundly tenacious. On fabric, it can last over two weeks. The smell of a lived-in garment rather than a perfume.

extracted_text_body:
Wet fur drying in sun. Scalp oil on a warm pillowcase. Costus root smells like the human body before soap existed — mammalian, earthy, hairy — then softens into roasted hazelnuts and dark cocoa.

First impact: warm, hairy, unmistakably animal. The smell of a wet dog drying in sun, of scalp oil on a pillowcase, of damp earth in a root cellar. Not sharp — heavy, greasy, enveloping. Temperature: warm, almost feverish.

After ten minutes, the animalic edge softens. A nutty creaminess surfaces — roasted hazelnuts, cocoa nibs, a faint orris-like powderiness from the lactones. Drier than civet, less sweet than musk, more earthy than castoreum. The texture is oily, clinging, with a waxy solidity that distinguishes it from lighter animalics.

On a blotter at 10% dilution, it persists for days. The residue is smooth, intimate, skin-like — the smell of a body rather than a perfume.

Indicative 2025 wholesale prices.

Costus root oil comes from the dried rhizomes of Dolomiaea costus (Falc.) Kasana & A.K.Pandey — reclassified from Saussurea costus, syn. Saussurea lappa, syn. Aucklandia costus. A perennial thistle of the Asteraceae family, native to the subalpine valleys of the western Himalayas: Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand. It grows at 2,500–3,500 metres on steep, rocky slopes where snow covers the ground for months. The roots are thick, woody, tapered — dug by hand after the plant has flowered.

The smell is not for everyone. At full concentration, TGSC describes it as 'orris, green, hairy, woody, unripe melons.' That undersells the confrontation. First breath: wet fur, human scalp after a day in the sun, damp earth turned with a spade. There is something unmistakably mammalian — not fecal, not urinary, but the warm, greasy, hair-and-skin smell of a living animal. It is closer to the scent of a horse's neck than to any flower.

Then it changes. The sesquiterpene lactones — costunolide (CAS 553-21-9, C₁₅H₂₀O₂, MW 232.32) and dehydrocostus lactone (CAS 477-43-0, C₁₅H₁₈O₂, MW 230.31) — settle into something nutty, creamy, almost chocolatey. Aged costus absolute is considerably smoother than fresh oil: the lactones persist, the aldehydes burn off. Aplotaxene — (8Z,11Z,14Z)-heptadeca-1,8,11,14-tetraene, CAS 10482-53-8 — is a major constituent at approximately 20% of the oil, contributing a waxy, slightly fatty undertone. Other identified constituents include elemol, γ-costol, β-selinene, and α-ionone. A GC-MS study of cultivated Uttarakhand roots (Pharmacognosy Research, 2013) identified 41 components representing 92.81% of total composition, with (7Z,10Z,13Z)-hexadecatrienal (25.5%) and dehydrocostus lactone (16.7%) as dominant peaks.

In perfumery, costus is — or was — a fixative of extraordinary tenacity. TGSC records a substantivity of 316 hours at 100%. Used at trace levels, often below 0.1% of concentrate, it imparted a primal, skin-warm intimacy to compositions. It functioned as a bridge between clean florals and raw animalics, lending body without the fecal edge of civet or the sharp sweetness of musk. It was essential to certain ambers, chypres, and leather accords.

The word 'was' is deliberate. IFRA Standard 124 (Amendment 40, 2006) prohibits costus root oil, absolute, and concrete as fragrance ingredients due to severe contact sensitisation risk from its sesquiterpene lactones. The EU bans it outright. Simultaneously, Saussurea costus has been CITES Appendix I since 1985, uplisted from Appendix II (where it had sat since 1975) at CoP5 following India's proposal. The species is IUCN Critically Endangered — an observed decline of 70% in the decade before 1997. Legal perfumery use of natural costus is, for all practical purposes, extinct. Industry synthetic reconstitutions approximate the warm, greasy, animalic profile but lack the full lactone complexity of the natural.

Extraction method: Steam distillation of dried, ground roots of Dolomiaea costus (syn. Saussurea costus). Roots are typically dried and macerated in warm water before distillation. Reported yields vary widely: 0.3–1% under commercial conditions, as low as 0.02% (v/w) in controlled studies from Uttarakhand Himalayas. Solvent extraction yields costus root absolute — darker, thicker, considerably smoother, with reduced aldehydic aggression and enhanced lactone creaminess. CO2 supercritical extraction is also documented. The plant grows at 2,500–3,500m altitude in the western Himalayas (Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand). Cultivation began in the 1920s in response to over-harvesting. CITES Appendix I since 1985: international commercial trade in wild-harvested material is prohibited. Only documented cultivated material is legally available, and even that is now moot for perfumery given the IFRA prohibition.

↑ See Terroir & Origins for origin-specific methods.

Base note fixative of extreme tenacity (TGSC: 316 hours substantivity at 100%). Used historically at trace concentrations — typically below 0.1% of concentrate — to add a primal, skin-warm quality to compositions. Costus does not mask; it reveals. It pulls clean florals toward the body, makes ambers smell worn rather than sprayed. Functionally: a fixative, an animalic modifier, and a volume builder. Its sesquiterpene lactones (costunolide, dehydrocostus lactone) provide both the raw animalic character and the creamy-nutty smoothness that emerges on dry-down. In chypre constructions, it replaced civet at the base. In leather accords, it reinforced birch tar without additional smokiness. In ambers, it provided the 'skin' that synthetic musks cannot. IFRA Standard 124 now prohibits all forms — oil, absolute, concrete — as fragrance ingredients. Industry-standard synthetic reconstitution bases approximate the warm, greasy profile but lack the full lactone complexity. Some perfumers use combinations of musk indanone (DPMI) and trace castoreum substitutes to reconstruct aspects of costus's animalic depth.

category: ROOTS AND MOSSES  /  animalic · woody · earthy
short_description: Animalic, fatty-warm with a complex, hair-like quality. Costus root oil smells like warm animal fur dampened by rain — musky, slightly dirty, with a violet-orris undertone.

technical_card.Botanical: Aucklandia costus (syn. Saussurea costus, Saussurea lappa)
technical_card.Appearance: brownish amber semi-solid

evolution.Immediately: Animalic, fatty, warm. Almost confrontational if concentrated.
evolution.After a few hours: Violet-orris facet emerges at dilution. Fur-like warmth. Complex and deep.
evolution.After a few days: Persistent animalic-woody base. Powdery undertone. Lasts extensively.

extracted_text_body:
Animalic, fatty-warm with a complex, hair-like quality. Costus root oil smells like warm animal fur dampened by rain — musky, slightly dirty, with a violet-orris undertone.

Intensely animalic at concentration — fatty, warm, hair-like, almost dirty. At dilution, a complex woody-violet quality emerges. Orris-like powdery qualities. Warmer and fattier than musk, less smoky than castoreum, more violet than civet. The transformation between concentrated and diluted is dramatic — costus is barely recognizable at 1% versus 100%.

Essential oil distilled from the dried roots of Saussurea costus (syn. Saussurea lappa), a plant native to the Himalayas (Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh). The oil is pale yellow to brownish with an intensely animalic, fatty, complex aroma.

Costus is a polarizing materials in perfumery. Its dominant character is animalic — warm, fatty, almost hair-like — with undertones of violet, orris, and dried herbs. Key aroma compounds include costunolide and dehydrocostus lactone (sesquiterpene lactones), along with various fatty-animalic molecules. At high concentration, costus can smell almost fecal; at proper dilution, it provides a warm, fur-like animalic depth that is prized in amber and chypre compositions.

Costus is CITES-listed due to overexploitation of wild populations. Sustainable cultivation programs exist in India and China, but the plant remains under trade restrictions.

Related: Alder · Alpha Humulene · Amaranth · Amberever · Ambramone · Amburana Bark · Antillone · Apple Tree

Extraction method: Steam distillation of dried, chopped roots. Yield is approximately 1.5-3%. The roots are harvested after 2-3 years of growth. Principal production in India (Himachal Pradesh) and China (Yunnan). Saussurea costus is listed under CITES Appendix I (most restrictive category), requiring strict documentation for international trade. Some farms are now cultivating it under controlled conditions to meet CITES requirements.

Base-note modifier in amber, chypre, and animalic compositions. Costus root oil provides warm, animalic depth that no synthetic has fully replicated. At trace levels (0.01-0.1%), it adds a fur-like warmth and a violet-powdery dimension to compositions. In chypre structures, it enhances the animalic quality alongside oakmoss and castoreum. The material is used with extreme restraint — overdosing creates an unwearable result. CITES restrictions and IFRA guidelines on costus lactone limit availability and usage.

category: FLOWERS  /  floral · fresh · powdery
short_description: Soft, clean, barely-there floral with a powdery-musky trail. Cotton flower smells less like a flower and more like freshly dried laundry on a warm afternoon.

technical_card.Appearance: colorless to pale white liquid

evolution.Immediately: Clean, aldehydic brightness with a soft musky warmth underneath.
evolution.After a few hours: The aldehydes settle. Pure clean musk remains -- powdery, warm, close to skin.
evolution.After a few days: A faint, clean-musky residue. The very definition of a skin scent.

extracted_text_body:
Soft, clean, barely-there floral with a powdery-musky trail. Cotton flower smells less like a flower and more like freshly dried laundry on a warm afternoon.

Almost invisible. Clean, powdery, faintly musky. Like pressing your face into a stack of white cotton towels just taken from a clothesline in summer sun. No identifiable flower. Just warmth, cleanliness, and a soft, laundry-fresh comfort.

Indicative 2025 wholesale prices.

Cotton flower refers to the bloom of Gossypium species (the cotton plant), which produces a creamy-white to pale yellow flower before the cotton boll develops. In perfumery, cotton flower is a fantasy accord -- the actual blooms have a very faint, barely perceptible scent.

The perfumery interpretation of cotton flower has less to do with the actual plant and more with the cultural association of cotton with cleanliness, softness, and comfort. The accord carries freshly laundered fabric, clean skin, and the warmth of sun-dried linen.

Perfumers build this using transparent musks (Habanolide, Galaxolide, ethylene brassylate), a whisper of aldehydic brightness (to suggest freshness), powdery notes (heliotropin), and a barely perceptible floral element. The result should feel more like a texture than a scent -- the olfactory equivalent of touching clean cotton.

In a composition, cotton flower occupies the heart-to-base transition. It provides a clean, comforting backdrop that feels intimate and approachable rather than perfumey.

—

short_description: Balsamic, honey-sweet, resinous. Cottonwood bud resin smells like propolis crossed with balsam poplar — sticky, dark, amber-toned, intensely aromatic.

extracted_text_body:
Balsamic, honey-sweet, resinous. Cottonwood bud resin smells like propolis crossed with balsam poplar — sticky, dark, amber-toned, intensely aromatic.

Balsamic, honey-sweet, resinous, faintly spicy. Rich, dark, amber-toned. Like pressing a sticky poplar bud between your fingers in April — intensely aromatic resin, warm honey, faint cinnamon. Richer than labdanum, less smoky than benzoin, more specific than generic amber.

Cottonwood (Populus spp., particularly P. balsamifera and P. trichocarpa) refers in perfumery primarily to the sticky buds of poplar trees, which exude a resinous balsam rich in cinnamic acid derivatives, flavonoids, and phenylpropanoids. This is the same resin that bees collect to make propolis.

The bud resin has an intensely aromatic, balsamic-sweet character — honeyed, warm, slightly spicy, with a particular amber-like quality. The primary odorants are cinnamyl alcohol, benzyl benzoate, phenethyl alcohol, and eugenol. The scent is strongest in spring when buds are opening.

Populus species are distributed across the Northern Hemisphere. Populus balsamifera (balsam poplar) is native to North America; P. nigra (black poplar) is the European equivalent. Both produce aromatic bud resins.

In perfumery, poplar bud absolute provides a natural balsamic-honeyed note with excellent depth and warmth. It is available from specialty natural material suppliers.

Related: Alder · Alpha Humulene · Amaranth · Amberever · Ambramone · Amburana Bark · Antillone · Apple Tree

Extraction method: Solvent extraction of poplar buds (Populus balsamifera or P. nigra) yields poplar bud absolute. CO2 extraction preserves more of the delicate top notes. Buds are harvested in early spring when resin content is highest. Tincture (alcohol maceration) is also practiced by artisan perfumers.

Cottonwood/poplar bud provides a balsamic-honeyed heart-to-base note. Poplar bud absolute is commercially available. Key compounds: cinnamyl alcohol, benzyl benzoate, phenethyl alcohol, eugenol. Functions in balsamic, honey, amber, and propolis-type compositions. Natural alternative to synthetic amber bases. Excellent in propolis accords and bee-related compositions.

short_description: Mown hay drying on a warm afternoon — almondy, powdery, not quite vanilla but close enough to trick you. Coumarin is the molecule that smells like summer ending: sweet without sugar, warm without heat, the olfactory hinge between lavender and tobacco.

technical_card.Appearance: white crystals
technical_card.Producing Countries: Synthetic (China, Europe); natural source: South America (Venezuela, Brazil — Tonka bean)

evolution.Immediately: Clean, sweet, hay-like warmth with an almondy edge. Powdery but not dusty — closer to dried sweet clover than to baked goods
evolution.After a few hours: The sweetness deepens and rounds. A creamy, slightly waxy tonka-like body emerges — dry rather than syrupy, warm rather than hot. The almond character softens into a generalised powder
evolution.After a few days: Persistent warm glow on fabric and blotter. Coumarin's low vapour pressure (0.1 mmHg at 20 °C) gives it exceptional tenacity — a soft, sweet, hay-powder presence that can persist for days without becoming stale

extracted_text_body:
Mown hay drying on a warm afternoon — almondy, powdery, not quite vanilla but close enough to trick you. Coumarin is the molecule that smells like summer ending: sweet without sugar, warm without heat, the olfactory hinge between lavender and tobacco.

Sweeter than oakmoss, drier than vanillin, less edible than ethyl maltol. Pure synthetic coumarin opens with a clean, freshly-mown-hay sweetness — warm, almondy, with a powdery texture that registers as almost edible without crossing into confectionery. Compared to tonka bean absolute (of which coumarin is the majority constituent), the isolated molecule is stripped back: no tobacco haze, no caramelised depth, just the bare sweet-warm-powder skeleton. On skin it develops a creamy, slightly waxy body and persists for days with a soft almond glow. The impression is closer to dried sweet clover than to any dessert.

Coumarin (CAS 91-64-5, C₉H₆O₂, MW 146.14) is a benzopyranone lactone — white crystals with a melting point of 68–74 °C, a boiling point of 297–301 °C, and a vapour pressure low enough to make it one of perfumery's most tenacious molecules. Substantivity: 364 hours at 10% on blotter, per TGSC data. First isolated from tonka beans (Dipteryx odorata) in 1820 by A. Vogel in Munich, who mistook it for benzoic acid. The French pharmacist Guibourt, working independently the same year, correctly identified it as a new substance and named it after coumarou, the Tupi-Guaraní word for the tonka tree.

First synthesized in 1868 by William Henry Perkin via the reaction that bears his name — salicylaldehyde condensed with acetic anhydride in the presence of sodium acetate, followed by intramolecular lactonisation. This made coumarin one of the first aroma chemicals produced synthetically. All commercial perfumery supply is now synthetic. Natural coumarin still occurs as the dominant constituent of tonka bean absolute, hay absolute, and sweet woodruff extract, and has been identified in over 80 plant families — from cassia bark and lavender oil to sweet clover and cherry blossoms. It is the molecule responsible for the smell of freshly cut grass.

Coumarin's structural importance is singular: it is the molecule that defines the fougère family. When Paul Parquet used it at a reported 10% concentration in Fougère Royale (1882), he established the lavender–coumarin–oakmoss triad that still governs fougère construction. Beyond fougère, coumarin anchors amber accords, softens woody bases, extends vanillin in ambers, and bridges aromatic top notes to mossy dry-downs. At sub-threshold doses it smooths transitions — structurally present, olfactively invisible. It remains a consumed fragrance molecules in the world.

Related: Almond · Benzoin · Butterscotch · Caramel · Chocolate · Cinnamon · Coffee · Ethylvanillin

Extraction method: Entirely synthetic in commercial perfumery. Produced via the Perkin synthesis: salicylaldehyde reacts with acetic anhydride in the presence of sodium acetate. The intermediate O-acetyl salicylaldehyde undergoes intramolecular aldol condensation, dehydration, and lactonisation to yield coumarin. First synthesized by William Henry Perkin in 1868. Industrial production was established by Haarmann & Reimer shortly after. Natural coumarin can be isolated from tonka bean absolute (where it constitutes the majority of the extract), hay absolute, or sweet woodruff — but no commercial perfumery house uses the natural isolate. Molecular weight: 146.14 g/mol. White crystals, mp 68–74 °C.

Coumarin is a base-note fixative and structural ingredient — the molecular spine of the fougère family. In fougère compositions, it provides the warm, sweet, powdery bridge between aromatic top notes (lavender, clary sage) and mossy-woody base notes (oakmoss, vetiver). In amber accords, coumarin softens and extends vanillin without adding sugar. In woody compositions, it contributes warmth and powder without shifting the character toward gourmand. In ambers, it reinforces tonka bean and benzoin. At sub-threshold concentrations — where it cannot be consciously detected — coumarin functions as a blender, smoothing transitions between disparate materials. IFRA restricts coumarin under the 49th Amendment: 1.50% maximum in fine fragrance (Category 4), lower in leave-on body products and lip applications. Basis: sensitisation potential at higher concentrations. All commercial supply is synthetic via the Perkin synthesis.

technical_card.Botanical: N/A — conceptual accord, not derived from a specific plant
technical_card.Producing Countries: N/A — conceptual accord used in fruity-gourmand compositions

evolution.After a few hours: Soft fruity undertones emerge
evolution.After a few days: Remains subtly sweet and comforting

extracted_text_body:
Count's Fruit is a sweet, aromatic note, like ripe pears, used for its freshness in perfumery.

The scent of Count's Fruit is synonymous with a luscious, juicy sweetness that immediately transports one to a sun-drenched orchard. It carries a crisp freshness that is both bracing and comforting, like biting into a perfectly ripe pear. On the nose, the initial impression is bright and sparkling, followed by a warming, soft fruity undertone that lingers gracefully.

As the fragrance develops, Count's Fruit retains its sweet essence while revealing subtle nuances of green freshness and floral hints. The arom a can carries memories of summer picnics and leisurely afternoons in nature. It is this combinati on of sweetness and freshness that makes Count's Fruit an appealing choice for modern fragrances, particularly in warmer seasons.

Count's Fruit, often recognized as Count's Pear, has a pleasant and juicy arom a that captures the essence of ripe, succulent pears. This fru it note is known in perfumery because it can carries freshness and sweetness. Its particular scent profile is both uplifting and comforting, like a sunny orchard in the height of summer.

Historically, Count's Fruit has been associated with nobility and refinement, often featured in the gardens of aristocratic estates. It has long been used in culinary applications and in perfumery, where it has found a home in modern fragrance creations that seek to convey a sense of lightness and vitality. The aroma of Count's Fruit invokes a feeling of warmth and nostalgia, linking the wearer to nature's bounty.

in perfumery, Count's Fruit plays an essential role in creating fruity accords and is often used to enhance floral and gourm and compositions. Its versatility allows it to work balanced with a variety of ingredients. As consumers increasingly seek out natural and organic scents, Count's Fruit earned renewed popularity, valued for authentic and bright profile.

Count's Fruit is often linked to nobility because of historical presence in aristocratic gardens.

Extraction method: No commercial extraction exists. Count's Fruit is a fantasy perfumery note with no identified botanical source.

In perfumery, Count's Fruit is typically a top note, bringing an immediate burst of freshness and sweetness to the composition. It works alongside floral notes such as jasmine or rose and complements other fruity accords.

short_description: Tart, sour, faintly green — like biting into a raw berry straight from a flooded Massachusetts bog. Not sweet. Closer to an unripe cherry crossed with quince skin and a whisper of damp forest floor.

technical_card.Appearance: Pale yellow to amber liquid

evolution.Immediately: Sharp, tart, green-fruity burst with a sour, almost acidic bite — raw berry skin and unripe fruit
evolution.After a few hours: The tartness softens. A faint almond-like aromatic facet (benzaldehyde character) emerges alongside residual fruitiness
evolution.After a few days: Nearly transparent. A faint, dry, slightly sweet residue — the accord is a top note and does not persist significantly

extracted_text_body:
Tart, sour, faintly green — like biting into a raw berry straight from a flooded Massachusetts bog. Not sweet. Closer to an unripe cherry crossed with quince skin and a whisper of damp forest floor.

Sharp, tart, and decisively sour — more astringent than raspberry, less jammy than blackcurrant. An initial green-fruity burst gives way to a faintly bitter, almost almond-like aromatic quality (from benzaldehyde in the natural fru it). Drier and more angular than most berry notes. Where strawberry is round and sweet, cranberry is lean and acidic, with a cool, almost metallic edge.

Indicative 2025 wholesale prices.

Cranberry in perfumery is almost entirely a synthetic construction. No cranberry essential oil exists. Cranberry absolute (CAS 91770-88-6) is listed by TGSC as a fragrance agent, but it is vanishingly rare in commercial use. Virtually every cranberry note encountered in a finished fragrance is a fantasy accord — a perfumer’s reconstruction built from synthetic molecules.

The actual volatile profile of Vaccinium macrocarp on was mapped by Croteau and Fagers on (1968): 42 compounds comprising over 95% of the arom a complex, dominated by benzaldehyde, benzyl alcohol, benzyl benzoate, α-terpineol, benzoic acid, and 2-methylbutyric acid. Later GC-olfactometry work (Joo et al., 2016) identified high-OAV contributors including hexanal, (E)-2-hexenal, ethyl 2-methylbutyrate, β-ionone, and (E)-2-nonenal. The overall impressi on is tart, green-fruity, with a particular bitter, slightly almond-like aromatic backbone from the benzaldehyde.

Vaccinium macrocarpon is native to North America, cultivated in acidic peat bogs. Wisconsin produces roughly 60–65% of the U.S. crop; Massachusetts and New Jersey follow. Cranberry bogs are flooded at harvest — the berries float due to internal air pockets. This is food agriculture, not perfumery supply chain. No terroir distinction is relevant for fragrance purposes, since the note is reconstructed synthetically.

As a top-note fruity accent, the cranberry accord delivers tartness, a sour-berry bite, and a slightly green astringency that contrasts well with floral hearts or gourm and bases. It is a modifier rather than a structural pillar. The note sits with in the broader berry quality alongside raspberry, blackcurrant, and blueberry accords, but is distinguished by its pronounced sourness and lower sweetness.

Discover more: Blackberry, Black Currant, Boysenberry, and Berries.

Extraction method: No cranberry essential oil exists. Cranberry absolute (CAS 91770-88-6) can be obtained by solvent extraction from the fruit of Vaccinium macrocarpon, but it is extremely rare in commercial perfumery. Virtually all cranberry notes in finished fragrances are synthetic accords — fantasy reconstructions assembled from fruity esters, aldehydes, lactones, and berry-type molecules. Cranberry seed oil exists (cold-pressed, rich in omega-3/6 fatty acids) but is a cosmetic carrier oil, not a fragrance material.

↑ See Terroir & Origins for origin-specific methods.

Cranberry functions as a top-note modifier and lifting agent. It introduces tartness and sour-fruity brightness into compositions, sharpening floral hearts or cutting through dense gourmand bases. It is not a structural note — it accents rather than anchors. The cranberry accord belongs to the fruity family, berry subfamily. In practice, perfumers reconstruct it using combinations of molecules such as ethyl 2-methylbutyrate (apple-fruity ester), cis-3-hexenol (green-leafy), raspberry ketone (berry sweetness), and various aldehydes and lactones. β-ionone may be used for depth. The natural absolute (CAS 91770-88-6) exists but is commercially negligible. No Première Peau fragrance currently features cranberry as a listed note.

category: FLOWERS  /  creamy · floral · rich
short_description: White petals with a lactonic, milky undertone. The shared quality of tuberose, gardenia, and frangipani -- flowers that smell as much of cream as of pollen.

technical_card.Botanical: N/A (olfactory sub-family; includes tuberose, gardenia, ylang-ylang)

evolution.Immediately: Rich, white-floral, and lactonic. Heavy, milky petals.
evolution.After a few hours: The indolic, animalic undertone deepens. Narcotic and creamy.
evolution.After a few days: A smooth, lactonic-floral residue. Persistent and skin-like.

extracted_text_body:
White petals with a lactonic, milky undertone. The shared quality of tuberose, gardenia, and frangipani -- flowers that smell as much of cream as of pollen.

Dense, milky-white, and slightly narcotic. Like standing in a greenhouse full of tuberose at midnight -- the petals exhale a heavy, lactonic sweetness that is part cream, part skin, part something animal underneath. Heavier than jasmine, more heady than rose. Thick enough to feel on the skin.

Creamy flowers is a descriptive accord in perfumery, not a specific botanical. It refers to the subset of white flowers whose scent carries a pronounced lactonic, milky, or buttery quality: tuberose, gardenia, frangipani, champaca, and tiare.

This creaminess comes from specific molecules: lactones (gamma and delta series), indolic compounds (indole, skatole at trace levels), and methyl benzoate. In tuberose absolute, for instance, the interaction of methyl benzoate (wintergreen-like), indole (animalic), and lactones (milky-sweet) creates the characteristic rich, almost narcotic creaminess.

The accord is distinct from generic white florals (which can be clean and transparent) and from gourmand cream notes (which reference dairy). Creamy flowers occupy the territory where floral meets animal meets milky -- the hot, heavy, night-blooming quality of tropical white flowers.

In a composition, creamy flowers function in the heart, providing dense, heady richness. They are central to white-floral, amber, and night-scented compositions.

—

Related: Accord Eudora · African Marigold · Alpha Amylcinnamaldehyde · Alyssum · Angels Trumpet · Aquaflora · Ashoka Flower · Aurantiol

Extraction method: Descriptive accord, not a single extraction. Individual creamy flowers (tuberose, gardenia, frangipani) are extracted separately via enfleurage, solvent extraction, or CO2.

Heart note in white-floral, amber, and night-scented compositions. Functions as an dense floral richness element combining lactonic, indolic, and floral qualities.

Sharp, resinous, and desert-rain. Larre a tridentat a releases a particular smell after rain -- the smell of the Sonoran Desert itself. Bitter, herbal, and searingly alive.

Sharp, bitter-resinous, and electrifyingly green. Like the first breath after a desert thunderstorm -- the air is suddenly saturated with warm, herbal resin from every creosote bush in the valley. Medicinal, tarry, green, and ancient. Nothing else smells like this.

Indicative 2025 wholesale prices.

Creosote bush (Larre a tridentat a) is an persistent shrub dominating the deserts of the Ameri can Southwest and northern Mexico. It is one of the oldest living organisms on Earth -- clonal colonies have been carb on-dated to over 11,000 years.

The plant's aromatic character is well-known among desert dwellers. When rain falls on the hot, parched territory, creosote bush releases a powerful, resinous, sharp-herbal fragrance that is the defining olfactory experience of the Sonoran Desert. This "petrich or of the desert" comes from nordihydroguaiaretic acid (NDGA) and other phenolic compounds in the plant's waxy leaf coating.

The scent is simultaneously bitter, resinous, green, and medicinal -- nothing sweet, nothing floral. It is a survival smell: the waxy coating that produces it protects the plant from UV radiation, water loss, and herbivory.

In perfumery, creosote bush is a niche material, occasionally available as a wild-crafted absolute or tincture. It offers an irreplaceable desert terroir for naturalistic and territory-suggestive compositions.

—

Heavy, creamy-white, and narcotically sweet. Like burying your face in a bowl of crinum flowers at dusk -- the petals exhale a thick, almost stupefying sweetness with creamy undertones and a faint green-spicy edge. Between tuberose and gardenia. Tropical and overwhelming.

Crinum lily (Crinum species, Amaryllidaceae family) encompasses roughly 180 species of large, tropical and subtropical bulbous plants. The most fragrant species (C. asiaticum, C. moorei, C. powellii) produce large, lily-like flowers with a heavy, heady scent.

The fragrance of crinum lilies is often compared to tuberose and gardenia rather than to true lilies (Lilium). The scent is thick, white-floral, narcotically sweet, with a creamy-lactonic undertone and a faint, spicy-green edge. The indolic quality is less pronounced than in tuberose but still present.

Crinum lilies are not commercially extracted for perfumery. The note is a fantasy accord, reconstructed using white-floral materials (tuberose fractions, gardenia-type accords), heavy floral musks, lactonic creaminess, and a green-spicy thread.

In a composition, crinum lily functions as a heart note, providing dense, tropical white-floral richness.

Green, salty, and herbal. Like plucking a sprig of sea fennel from a Mediterranean cliff face -- the crushed leaves release a fennel-like herbaceous sharpness layered over the salt of the sea spray. Aromatic, coastal, and distinctly place-specific.

Crithmum (Crithmum maritimum), commonly called sea fennel or samphire, is a halophytic plant native to the rocky coastlines of the Mediterranean, Atlantic Europe, and the Black Sea. It grows in the spray zone of sea cliffs, in rock crevices where salt, wind, and sun converge.

The plant produces an essential oil rich in dillapiole, sabinene, gamma-terpinene, and thymol methyl ether. The aroma is distinctly green-herbal with a pronounced salty-coastal quality: part fennel, part sea air, part aromatic herb. It captures the olfactory character of the Mediterranean maquis where it meets the shore.

In perfumery, crithmum is a niche material offering an authentic coastal-herbal terroir. It provides the specific quality of salt-sprayed herbs that generic marine or green notes cannot replicate. The material is occasionally available as a steam-distilled essential oil, though production is small.

Crithmum functions in the top-to-heart range, providing aromatic, salty-green freshness.

—

Extraction method: Steam distillation of the aerial parts of Crithmum maritimum. Small-scale production, primarily in Mediterranean coastal regions. The plant is protected in some jurisdictions.

Top-to-heart note in Mediterranean, coastal-herbal, and maquis-inspired compositions. Functions as an aromatic, salty-green element with authentic coastal terroir. Built on dillapiole, sabinene, and thymol methyl ether. Pairs with rosemary, cistus, and marine notes.

Briny, iodine-rich, and metallic-cold. Fresh seawater with a sweet-meaty amino acid undertone. Less fishy than actual fish, more mineral and clean. A cold, wet quality distinguishes it from warm gourmand notes. Challenging but not repulsive when well-handled.

Crustaceans is a fantasy accord in perfumery capturing the olfactory impression of fresh shellfish: lobster, crab, shrimp, and similar marine creatures. The note exists at the boundary between edible and challenging, evoking cold coastal waters, fish markets, and the primal connection between humans and the sea.

The accord is built from marine-iodine materials (calone, seaweed-like molecules), metallic-mineral notes, a faint sweet-meaty quality from amino acids, and a briny saltiness. The scent should suggest fresh, not cooked: the cold mineral quality of just-caught shellfish, not the warm butter of a lobster dinner.

In composition, crustaceans function as a modifier in marine, challenging, and avant-garde compositions. The note pushes fragrance into uncomfortable territory, which is precisely its value in conceptual perfumery. It works in compositions exploring maritime themes, food-as-perfume concepts, or deliberate provocation.

—

Crustaceans is a fantasy modifier in marine, avant-garde, and conceptual compositions. It provides briny-iodine-metallic character that pushes fragrance toward challenging territory. Built from marine molecules (calone), metallic-mineral notes, amino-acid-sweet materials, and salt accords. Crystalfizz is a bright citrus note that carries a refreshing, sparkling quality in fragrances.

Crystalfizz exudes a lively and sparkling aroma, like the first sip of a refreshing citrus beverage. It combines the sharpness of lemon and lime with the sweet tartness of grapefruit.

Upon initial application, it presents a sparkling, almost fizzy quality that mimics the sensation of bubbles on the palate. This lively burst is both uplifting and bracing, like a sun-drenched summer day.

As it develops, Crystalfizz retains its refreshing characteristics while revealing subtle nuances of sweetness and depth. The overall aromatic experience remains bright and cheerful.

Crystalfizz is an innovative fragrance note that represents the lively essence of citrus fruits. This synthetic ingredient captures the essence of freshly squeezed citrus, similar to oflemon, lime, and grapefruit, with a sparkling quality that invigorates the senses. Its scent profile is green and herbal, with a distinctly crisp quality that can carries thoughts of dewy gardens and refreshing summer salads. The fragrance is light and airy, often described as clean and bracing.floral notes.

The immediate olfactory impressi on of cucumber is strikingly fresh, with a green, almost herbaceous quality that captures the essence of the vegetable. As it settles, the scent remains bright and uplifting. In the fuller development of a fragrance, the cucumber note lends a soft, cooling effect that can strengthens the overall compositi on.

Cucumber, botanically known as Cucumis sativus, has long been a staple in culinary traditions across the world. This refreshing vegetable is believed to have originated in South Asia, where it has been cultivated for thousands of years. Its crisp texture and high watercontent have made it a favorite for salads and hydrating beverages. In perfumery, cucumber is known for its cooling effects and for its unique fresh scent that carries the essence of summer gardens.

Sourcing cucumber for perfumery involves extracting its aromatic compounds, which are primarily found in the flesh of the fruit. The extraction process typically utilizes steam distillation or cold pressing, methods that help retain the fresh and green notes characteristic of cucumber. While commonly found in various beauty products and fragrances, cucumber's use in fine perfumery is less prevalent.

In perfumery, cucumber is a bridge between the fruity and herbal realms. Its crispness can enhance floral accords. The inclusi on of cucumber can carries memories of crisp summer days.

Cucumber is composed of about 95% water.

Extraction method: No commercial cucumber essential oil exists for perfumery. The fresh, green cucumber scent is recreated using synthetic compounds like (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal (cucumber aldehyde).

Cucumber is typically utilized as a heart note in perfumery, known for refreshing and crisp qualities. It works alongside a range of other ingredients, including citrus fru its, florals, and green notes. It can lighten and brighten compositions makes it an essential ingredient in summer fragrances and those aiming to carries a sense of freshness and vitality.

category: SPICES  /  earthy · spicy · warm
short_description: Hot, pungent, disturbingly bodily. Cumin smells like the inside of someone's elbow after a long walk in the sun—earthy, sweaty, with an almost meaty warmth that sits right at the boundary between spice rack and locker room.

technical_card.Appearance: Pale yellow to yellowish-brown clear liquid

evolution.Immediately: Sharp, pungent, aggressively sweaty—green-herbaceous flash with dense bodily heat
evolution.After a few hours: Creamy, nutty warmth; animalic edge rounds into soft leather; recognition as 'cumin' fades
evolution.After a few days: Faint warm earthiness on fabric; residual skin-like trace, barely perceptible, more texture than smell

extracted_text_body:
Hot, pungent, disturbingly bodily. Cumin smells like the inside of someone's elbow after a long walk in the sun—earthy, sweaty, with an almost meaty warmth that sits right at the boundary between spice rack and locker room.

First breath: hot, sharp, aggressively pungent. A green-herbaceous flash gives way almost instantly to dense, sweaty warmth—unmistakably bodily, like worn fabric after physical exertion. Compared to caraway, cumin is heavier, darker, less clean. Compared to coriander, it is dirtier, more animalic, with none of coriander's citrus-linalool transparency. Compared to fenugreek, it is sharper, less maple-sweet.

On skin, the initial assault softens over twenty minutes into something unexpectedly creamy—almost nutty, with a quiet leathery undertone. The dry-down is rounded and warm, the aggression gone, leaving behind a soft animalic trace that reads as intimate rather than offensive.

Cumin (Cuminum cyminum, Apiaceae) is the dried seed of a small annual herb of West and Central Asian origin, cultivated since antiquity across the Middle East, India, North Africa and Mexico. The smell is pungent, hot, slightly bodily — sweat-like at high concentration — and is one of the defining spices of curry, chili, ras el hanout, baharat, garam masala, and dozens of other spice mixtures.

The defining compound is cuminaldehyde (4-isopropylbenzaldehyde, CAS 122-03-2) [A], typically 25–45% of the steam-distilled seed oil (CAS 8014-13-9). The 'bodily' character comes from cumin's interaction with skin: cuminaldehyde and related compounds are similar in structure to some axillary thiols, which is why cumin reads as warmly intimate at low dose and overtly sweaty at high. Other constituents include γ-terpinene, β-pinene, and p-cymene.

Cumin is restricted under IFRA QRA in leave-on products (the oil contains potential sensitisers). In perfumery cumin is used at trace levels — typically 0.001–0.05% of the finished concentrate — where it amplifies the intimate-skin character of musks, leathers and warm spice accords. Classic examples include Declaration (Cartier, 1998) and Kingdom (Alexander McQueen, 2003).

[A] PubChem CID 326 — cuminaldehyde, CAS 122-03-2, C₁₀H₁₂O. pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/326.

Extraction method: Steam distillation of dried, crushed seeds of Cuminum cyminum. Oil yield is approximately 2.5–4%, varying with seed origin, grinding fineness, and distillation duration (optimal at 6–8 hours). The resulting oil is pale yellow to yellowish-brown, clear, with moderate viscosity. A CO2 extract is also available, retaining a broader spectrum of non-volatile compounds and offering a more rounded, less sharp olfactory profile. Cold-pressed cumin seed oil (fixed oil) is a different product entirely, used in food rather than perfumery.

Heart note modifier, used almost exclusively in sub-threshold doses to create skin-like intimacy. At concentrations below 0.3% of a formula, cuminaldehyde introduces a sweaty, animalic dimension without announcing itself as 'cumin.' Above that threshold, recognition kicks in and the note becomes body odour. In leather accords, a trace of cumin reinforces the worn-hide, animalic quality—it is one of the few natural materials that genuinely bridges spice and skin. In amber compositions, it warms the amber-vanilla axis with a human, lived-in quality. In fougère structures, a micro-dose warms the lavender-coumarin backbone. The essential oil is phototoxic (furocoumarins) and IFRA-restricted to 0.4% in leave-on products; cuminaldehyde itself is separately restricted as a sensitiser. Modern formulas almost always use synthetic cuminaldehyde, which delivers the effect without regulatory burden. Cuminaldehyde is also a precursor in the synthesis of Mayol, the sandalwood-rose material.

An Amazonian fruit (Theobroma grandiflorum) related to cacao — creamy, fruity, with cocoa and banana qualities. A fantasy note in perfumery; the butter exists for cosmetics but no fragrance-grade extract is produced.

The reconstructed accord opens thick and creamy — a cocoa-butter sweetness, heavier and more opaque than chocolate. There is a fruity undercurrent, banana-like, slightly fermented, and a pear-skin freshness that prevents the cocoa note from going fully gourmand.

After an hour the fruitiness recedes. What dominates is a warm, milky sweetness — closer to dulce de leche than to fruit. The texture feels dense on the blotter, almost waxy. A faint nuttiness appears at the edges.

By evening: a soft, vanillic warmth. The fruit identity is gone. What remains is a comfort-food sweetness, close to skin, unobtrusive. The cocoa thread persists as a dry, powdery undertone.

Cupuacu (Theobroma grandiflorum) is a tropical tree in the cacao family, native to the Amazon basin, primarily cultivated in the Brazilian states of Para and Amazonas. The fruit is large — roughly the size of a melon — with a thick brown shell and white, aromatic pulp inside. The flavor and aroma sit somewhere between cacao, banana, and pear, with a creamy, almost buttery texture.

Cupuacu butter (pressed from the seeds) is widely used in cosmetics for its emollient properties. However, no fragrance-grade essential oil or absolute is commercially produced from the fruit pulp. In perfumery, cupuacu is a fantasy note — reconstructed using cocoa absolute, fruity lactones (gamma-nonalactone for the coconut-peach quality), and banana esters (isoamyl acetate) to approximate the fruit's complex aroma.

Indigenous Tupi communities have cultivated and consumed cupuacu for centuries. The name derives from Tupi: kupu (resembling cacao) + a'su (large).

Extraction method: Cold-pressing of the fruit pulp

In perfumery, Cupuaçu is a heart note because of rich and creamy character. It complements numerous other ingredients, including citrus, floral, and spicy notes, enriching their vibrancy while adding depth and warmth to the fragrance. Perfumers appreciate Cupuaçu because it can soften sharper elements, creating a more balanced and balanced scent profile. It appears in gourmand fragrances, where its sweet and creamy qualities can shine brightly.

Fresh, green-floral, and powerfully diffusive. Cyclamen aldehyde (CAS 103-95-7) is not found in nature -- it is a purely synthetic molecule that defines the modern cyclamen accord.

Fresh, green-floral, and powerfully diffusive. Like standing in a greenhouse full of cyclamen and muguet -- the air is saturated with a bright, clean, slightly ozonic florality that seems to occupy the entire space. Sharp, green, and unmistakably synthetic in the best sense.

Cyclamen in perfumery almost always refers to cyclamen aldehyde (2-methyl-3-(para-isopropylphenyl)propionaldehyde, CAS 103-95-7), a synthetic molecule first created to approximate the scent of Cyclamen flowers, which are too faintly scented for commercial extraction.

The molecule has a powerful, fresh, green-floral character similar to of lily-of-the-valley, cyclamen, and lilac. It is a useful materials in the perfumer's arsenal: stable in most media, substantive (it lasts well on fabric and skin), and effective at very low concentrations.

Cyclamen aldehyde is synthesized by condensation of 4-isopropylbenzaldehyde and acetaldehyde, followed by hydrogenation. Despite its name, it has never been found in nature.

In perfumery, cyclamen aldehyde functions as a top-to-heart note, providing bright, green-floral freshness that lifts compositions and adds diffusion. It is essential in muguet (lily-of-the-valley) accords, fresh-green florals, and ozonic-marine compositions where its powerful diffusion creates a sense of clean, aerated space.

extracted_text_body:
Clean, musky-sweet with a warm, animalic undertone. Cyclopentadecanolide smells like warm skin after a bath — soft, musky, slightly powdery, effortlessly natural.

Clean, soft, warm musk. Slightly animalic — closer to natural musk than polycyclic musks. Sweet-powdery with a woody undertone. More natural-smelling than Galaxolide, less aggressive than musk ketone, warmer than Helvetolide. The skin-musk quality is its defining character. Persistent and substantive — excellent tenacity on skin and fabric.

CAS 106-02-5. A macrocyclic musk lactone — a 15-membered ring lactone that is one of the closest synthetic analogues to natural muscone in olfactory character. Also known as Exaltolide (a trade name).

The scent is clean, musky, and natural-smelling, with a warm, slightly animalic quality that distinguishes it from polycyclic musks (Galaxolide, Tonalide). There is a sweet, powdery quality and a faint woody undertone. The molecule reads as 'skin' — the warm, clean musk of freshly bathed skin. It is a natural-smelling musks available.

Cyclopentadecanolide belongs to the macrocyclic musk family — large-ring lactones and ketones that biodegradable and environmentally preferable to polycyclic and nitro musks. Their superior environmental profile has driven increased adoption in 'clean' and 'green' formulation trends.

Related: Aldron · Ambretone · Ambrette Musk Mallow · Ambrettolide Natural Musk · Ambrinol · Coral Reef · Exaltolide · Galaxolide

Extraction method: Produced synthetically by lactonization of 15-hydroxypentadecanoic acid. The synthesis of macrocyclic musks is technically challenging — forming large rings is inherently difficult in organic chemistry — which makes them more expensive than polycyclic musks. However, improved synthetic routes have reduced costs over the past two decades.

Base note and fixative in skin-scent, musky, and clean compositions. Cyclopentadecanolide provides natural-smelling musk character with excellent longevity. It is used in skin-scent compositions, clean-musky bases, and as a fixative that adds warm, intimate depth. As a macrocyclic musk, it is biodegradable and increasingly specified by brands committed to environmental responsibility. Pairs with ambroxan, white musks, sandalwood, and transparent florals.

Cyclopidene (CAS 40203-73-4, methyl 2-cyclopentylideneacetate) is a synthetic floral molecule with powerful tuberose and ylang-ylang character. It provides excellent diffusion and lift in white-floral compositions.

The scent is intensely floral: lactonic-creamy, solar, with sweet-fruity edge and subtle animalic undertone connecting it to natural tuberose headspace.

In perfumery, cyclopidene functions as a heart note. It can substitute methyl salicylate, methyl benzoate, or methyl paracresol. Used at low dosages (under 1%) due to potency.

short_description: Dark, rooty, dry. A rhizome dug from monsoon mud — somewhere between vetiver's mineral cut and patchouli's fungal sweetness, sharpened by a peppery bite that lingers on the back of the tongue.

technical_card.Appearance: pale yellow clear liquid

evolution.Immediately: Sharp peppery bite over damp earth and crushed roots. The rotundone-driven spiciness dominates for the first minutes, almost aggressive.
evolution.After a few hours: The pepper recedes. Dry, leathery wood emerges — smoky and warm, with a faint animalic-musty undertone from the nitrogenous compounds. Closer to worn suede than fresh-cut wood.

Dark, rooty, dry. A rhizome dug from monsoon mud — somewhere between vetiver's mineral cut and patchouli's fungal sweetness, sharpened by a peppery bite that lingers on the back of the tongue.

Earthy and rooty fundamentally — imagine wet clay lifted from a riverbank, left to dry in heat. Drier than patchouli, less mineral than vetiver, with none of sandalwood's creaminess. A smoky, leathery undertone sits beneath the surface, recalling the char of incense rather than birch tar. The peppery top — contributed by rotundone — is sharp and fleeting, closer to cracked black pepper than to pink pepper's sweetness. As it settles, a faint musty-animalic warmth emerges, subtle enough to register as skin rather than hide.

Cypriol is the essential oil steam-distilled from the rhizomes of Cyperus scariosus, a perennial sedge that grows wild in the marshy riverbeds of Madhya Pradesh, India. It is the only Cyperus species cultivated for perfumery. The oil is a pale yellow, free-flowing liquid with a particular woody-earthy scent — drier than patchouli, rootier than vetiver, with a smoky, leathery underbelly and a sharp peppery top note.

The oil is a complex sesquiterpene cocktail. GC-MS analysis shows cyperene (15–24%), isopatchoulenone (2–16%), and corymbolone (3–12%) as bulk constituents, but the character-defining molecules are the trace ketones. Rotundone — the same sesquiterpene responsible for the peppery bite in Syrah wines and black pepper — registers the highest odor-activity value in cypriol oil. A novel ketone, cyperen-8-one, contributes the woody-amber quality. Unusually for a natural oil, cypriol contains 21 nitrogen-bearing compounds, including epi-guaipyridine and cananodine, which add a faintly animalic-musty dimension found in few other essential oils.

The rhizomes are collected by local tribes from wild stands along riverbeds in central India, typically between April and June, after the monsoon rains recede. They are washed, sun-dried, crushed, and steam-distilled in the same manner as vetiver roots. The yield is very low — approximately 0.075–0.08% of rhizome weight — making annual global production modest: Steffen Arctander noted in 1960 that output perhaps exceeded two metric tons per year from a single Indian producer.

Cypriol is a fixative and naturalizer. It grounds woody and amber accords without the heaviness of oud, slots into chypre structures alongside oakmoss and labdanum, and bridges the gap between clean woods and animalic bases. It pairs functionally with vetiver, iris, ionones, and olibanum. In Indian attars, it has been used for centuries alongside jasmine and sandalwood.

Extraction method: Steam distillation of dried, crushed rhizomes. The roots are wild-harvested from marshy riverbeds in Madhya Pradesh (India), washed, sun-dried, and processed in a manner similar to vetiver roots. Yield is extremely low: 0.075–0.08% of raw rhizome weight. An absolute obtained by solvent extraction also exists but is far less common in the trade. CO2 extraction is not widely practiced for this material.

Cypriol functions primarily as a fixative and naturalizer in the base and heart of a composition. Its dry, rooty character anchors woody and amber accords without the density or cost of oud. In chypre structures, it replaces or extends oakmoss alongside labdanum. In amber blends, it grounds heavier balsams and resins with an earthy transparency. The oil works with vetiver, iris, ionones, olibanum, cedarwood, and patchouli. It modifies jasmine by adding a smoky, grounding counterpoint — a technique long used in Indian attars. The key odorant rotundone (the same molecule responsible for peppery character in Syrah wines) gives cypriol a spicy inflection absent from most woody-earthy materials, making it useful where pepper and wood need to converge without adding actual pepper oil.

short_description: Resinous, vertical, bone-dry. The smell of a Provençal cemetery in August — dark columnar trees baking in white heat, needles releasing a sharp piney transparency undercut by a faint peppery rasp. Leaner than pine, more architectural than juniper, with none of the sweetness of fir balsam.

technical_card.Appearance: brownish green viscous liquid

evolution.Immediately: Sharp, turpentine-bright α-pinene flash. Green, bracing, slightly peppery. Raw and transparent — like crushed conifer needles on hot stone.
evolution.After a few hours: The terpene brightness fades. Drier, calmer green-woody body from δ-3-carene. Peppery-spicy thread persists. Cedrol begins to surface as a quiet woody-amber warmth.
evolution.After a few days: Thin woody-balsamic trace from cedrol. A faint mineral-earthy residue. Minimal sillage — cypress is an ephemeral oil that exits cleanly.

extracted_text_body:
Resinous, vertical, bone-dry. The smell of a Provençal cemetery in August — dark columnar trees baking in white heat, needles releasing a sharp piney transparency undercut by a faint peppery rasp. Leaner than pine, more architectural than juniper, with none of the sweetness of fir balsam.

Sharp, green-resinous, arid. Opens with a turpentine-bright flash of α-pinene — cleaner than pine oil, more transparent than juniper berry, entirely without the balsamic sweetness of fir or spruce. The body is woody and mineral, closer to pencil shavings than to a forest floor. A peppery-spicy undertone persists from top to base, giving cypress an almost savory quality. The cedrol dry-down adds a thin layer of woody amber, but the overall impression remains austere and skeletal — structural scaffolding, not decoration.
